client: I've been really struggling since my grandmother passed away last month. I just can't seem to focus on anything for university — I'll sit down to study and then suddenly I'm just staring at the wall, feeling this heavy sadness that I can't shake. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to help, honestly, because nothing is going to bring her back.
therapist: What you're carrying right now sounds incredibly heavy — grief has a way of pulling the ground out from under us, especially when it hits in the middle of demanding responsibilities like university. I hear some doubt about whether talking can really help, and that's a completely understandable place to be when the pain feels this raw and final. I'm wondering, even if it can't change what's happened, what might it feel like to have a space where you don't have to carry this quite so alone?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I guess... the idea of not carrying it alone sounds nice in theory, but I'm not sure I actually know how to let someone else in when it comes to this. Like, I've tried talking to friends about losing my dad and it just ends up feeling worse — they say the wrong thing or get uncomfortable and then I feel guilty for even bringing it up. So part of me wonders if this will just be more of the same, you know?
therapist: It sounds like you've been hurt before when you reached out, and now you're protecting yourself from that happening again — which makes a lot of sense given what you've experienced. I notice there's something quite tender in the way you're sharing this, like a part of you still hopes this could be different, even while another part is bracing for disappointment. Can you tell me a little more about what "letting someone in" would need to look like for it to actually feel safe, rather than leaving you feeling worse?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I think you're right that there's still a part of me that hopes things could be different, but it's really hard to even imagine what "safe" would look like anymore. Every time I've opened up to someone, it either felt like they were just waiting for me to stop talking so they could move on, or they used what I shared against me later. I guess for it to feel safe, I'd need to know the person actually has the capacity to stay, not just show up when it's convenient for them.
therapist: What you've just described — needing someone who will *stay* — feels like such a core and deeply human need, and it makes complete sense given how many times you've been left holding the weight alone. I notice you're speaking quite softly as you share this, and I want you to know that what you're saying matters and I'm not going anywhere. I'm curious — when you think about those past experiences where people didn't stay, do you find that shapes how you see yourself, not just how you see others?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: Yeah... I think it does shape how I see myself, more than I'd like to admit. Like somewhere along the way I started believing that people leave because there's something fundamentally wrong with me, something I can't quite fix or hide well enough. It's not a thought I walk around consciously having, but it's there underneath everything, kind of like a hum you stop noticing until someone points it out.
therapist: That "hum" you described is such a powerful way to put it — it's often those quiet, background beliefs that end up shaping so much of how we move through the world without us even realising it. What you've just named, that belief that something is fundamentally wrong with you, is something we could really gently explore together, because beliefs like that usually have a story behind them and they're not the same as the truth. I'm wondering, when do you think you first started hearing that hum?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I've been sitting with that question and... I think it started pretty early, maybe around middle school when I just never seemed to fit in with anyone. I remember always watching other kids laugh together and feeling like there was some instruction manual everyone else had been given that I somehow missed. It's weird to say out loud because part of me is already bracing for you to tell me that's just a distorted thought, and I'm not sure I'm ready to have it dismissed that easily.
therapist: I want you to know that I have no intention of dismissing what you just shared — that image of watching other kids from the outside, feeling like you missed something everyone else was handed, that's not just a "distorted thought" to be corrected, it's a real and painful experience that shaped how you came to understand yourself. It took courage to share that and then name your fear about how I'd respond, all in the same breath. Can you tell me more about what that little version of you made sense of in those moments — what conclusions did they start drawing about why they didn't fit?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I think that little version of me decided pretty early on that there must be something fundamentally wrong with me, like I was missing some ingredient that everyone else had. It wasn't just that I was shy or awkward — it felt more like I was built differently, and other people could somehow sense that and kept their distance because of it. And the worst part is, even now as an adult, I still catch myself believing that same thing when I'm in a room full of people and feel invisible.
therapist: That belief — that you were built differently, that others could somehow *sense* it — has clearly followed you from that middle school hallway all the way into the rooms you stand in today, and that's such a long time to carry something so heavy. I notice there's a real intensity in how you're sharing this, like this isn't just something you're recalling but something you're still *feeling* right now. I want to gently ask — when you're in that room feeling invisible, what would it mean about you if that feeling were actually telling the truth?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, fast speech

client: If that feeling were telling the truth... I guess it would mean that I really am just fundamentally less interesting, less worth knowing than other people. Like there's something quietly wrong with me that everyone can detect but nobody says out loud. And honestly, sitting here right now, part of me does believe that's true — it doesn't feel like a distortion, it feels like just... reality.
therapist: Thank you for trusting me with that — and I want to sit with it for a moment rather than rush to reassure you, because what you just said deserves to be heard, not immediately fixed. That belief feels like reality *because* it's been with you for so long, quietly confirmed every time someone left or didn't show up, which is exactly how our deepest beliefs about ourselves get cemented — not because they're true, but because life kept handing you experiences that seemed to prove them. I'm wondering, if a close friend described themselves to you the way you just described yourself, what would you feel toward them?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I'd probably feel really sad for them, and want to tell them that they're wrong about themselves. But it's different when it's me — like, I can extend that kind of compassion to someone else pretty easily, but when I turn it inward it just feels... fake, or like I'm lying to myself. I don't know why it's so hard to believe the same things about myself that I'd believe about someone else.
therapist: What you just noticed — that gap between the compassion you can offer others and the wall that goes up when you try to turn it inward — is actually one of the most important things we could explore together, and you've named it so clearly. I notice you're speaking quite quickly as you share this, like part of you is moving fast through something that might feel vulnerable to slow down in. I'm curious — when you try to offer yourself that same kindness and it feels "fake," what do you imagine you'd have to give up or admit if you actually let yourself believe it?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: That question kind of stops me, honestly. Like, if I actually let myself believe I deserve kindness, I think I'd have to admit that I've been really hard on myself for a long time, and maybe that... that wasn't necessary? And that feels almost worse, because then what was the point of all that suffering I put myself through.
therapist: What you just touched on is profound and painful in equal measure — that if the harshness wasn't necessary, it might mean all that suffering didn't have to happen, and that's genuinely a grief of its own. There's something in your voice right now that sounds like you're holding a lot as you sit with that realisation, even as the words come quickly. I want to stay right here with you in this — what do you think that younger version of you, the one who first decided something was wrong with them, was actually trying to do by being so hard on themselves?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I think... that younger version of me was just trying to make sense of why people kept leaving, or not showing up, or making me feel like I was too much. If I could find the flaw in myself, I could fix it, and then maybe things would be different. It felt like control, I guess, even though it was actually just... a way of punishing myself for something that probably wasn't even my fault.
therapist: What you just said is really significant — that the self-criticism was never really about finding the truth, it was about finding *control* in situations where you had very little, and that's such a compassionate and wise thing to recognise about yourself. I notice you're speaking quite quickly, like these words are coming from somewhere deep and you're moving through them fast — and I just want to slow down for a moment, because what you said at the end, that it probably wasn't even your fault, deserves to be heard more fully. How does it feel to say that out loud — that it wasn't your fault?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech
